title: Γεωργὸς καὶ φυτόν
part: The Farmer and the Tree (Chambry 85 · Perry 299)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 85 (= Perry 299). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Φυτὸν ἦν εἰς γεωργοῦ χώραν, καρπὸν μὴ φέρον, ἀλλὰ μόνον στρουθῶν καὶ τεττίγων κελαδούντων ἦν καταφυγή.
sentences.tr: Phyton ēn eis geōrgou chōran, karpon mē pheron, alla monon strouthōn kai tettigōn keladountōn ēn kataphygē.
sentences.l: There was a tree on a farmer's land, bearing no fruit, but it was only a refuge for sparrows and chirping cicadas.
sentences.i: There was a tree on a farmer's land that bore no fruit; it was nothing but a refuge for sparrows and shrilling cicadas.
sentences.n: φυτόν is anything planted, plant or tree; the axe and the bees later decide that this one is a tree. εἰς with the accusative stands where classical Attic wants ἐν with the dative — later Greek lets the two prepositions run together, and Chambry prints what he found. μή rather than οὐ with the participle makes it a description of the kind of tree it is, not a report about a particular occasion.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ γεωργὸς ὡς ἄκαρπον ἐκτεμεῖν ἤμελλεν.
sentences.tr: Ho de geōrgos hōs akarpon ektemein ēmellen.
sentences.l: And the farmer was about to cut it down as fruitless.
sentences.n: ὡς with the predicate accusative ἄκαρπον again gives the man's own ground for acting — 'on the view that it was fruitless'.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ τὸν πέλεκυν λαβὼν ἐπέφερε τὴν πληγήν.
sentences.tr: Kai dē ton pelekyn labōn epephere tēn plēgēn.
sentences.l: And there and then, having taken the axe, he was bringing the blow to bear.
sentences.i: And so he took the axe and set about striking.
sentences.n: καὶ δή marks the step actually taken, not merely intended. The imperfect ἐπέφερε leaves the blow in progress — which is what gives the birds their opening.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ τέττιγες καὶ οἱ στρουθοὶ ἱκέτευον τὴν καταφυγὴν αὐτῶν μὴ ἐκκόψαι, ἀλλ᾽ ἐᾶσαι, ὥστε ᾄδειν ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ σὲ τὸν γεωργὸν τέρπειν.
sentences.tr: Hoi de tettiges kai hoi strouthoi hiketeuon tēn kataphygēn autōn mē ekkopsai, all’ easai, hōste āidein en autōi kai se ton geōrgon terpein.
sentences.l: And the cicadas and the sparrows kept beseeching him not to cut down their refuge, but to let it be, so that they might sing in it and delight you, the farmer.
sentences.n: ἱκετεύω is the verb of formal supplication, what a suppliant does at an altar; the imperfect keeps them pleading while the axe is up. Mid-sentence the Greek slides out of report into direct address — σὲ τὸν γεωργόν, 'you, the farmer', where a strict report would say 'him'. Chambry prints it so, and this collection does it often enough that it is a habit rather than a slip. ὥστε with the infinitive gives the result they intend.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ μηδὲν αὐτῶν φροντίσας, καὶ δευτέραν πληγὴν καὶ τρίτην ἐπέφερε.
sentences.tr: Ho de mēden autōn phrontisas, kai deuteran plēgēn kai tritēn epephere.
sentences.l: But he, having taken no thought at all of them, brought on both a second blow and a third.
sentences.i: But he paid them no attention at all, and brought down a second blow and a third.
sentences.n: φροντίζω takes the genitive of what one gives thought to; μηδέν is an internal accusative — not 'nothing' but 'not at all'.

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ ἐκοίλανε τὸ δένδρον, σμῆνος μελισσῶν καὶ μέλι εὗρε.
sentences.tr: Hōs de ekoilane to dendron, smēnos melissōn kai meli heure.
sentences.l: And when he had hollowed out the tree, he found a swarm of bees and honey.
sentences.n: σμῆνος is the swarm and the hive together. Wild bees nesting in a hollow trunk were an ordinary source of honey, and honey was the chief sweetener the Greek kitchen had — so what he has found is worth more than fruit.

sentences.t: Γευσάμενος δὲ τὸν πέλεκυν ἔρριψε καὶ τὸ φυτὸν ἐτίμα ὡς ἱερὸν καὶ ἐπεμελεῖτο.
sentences.tr: Geusamenos de ton pelekyn erripse kai to phyton etima hōs hieron kai epemeleito.
sentences.l: And having tasted it, he threw the axe away and began to honour the tree as sacred and to care for it.
sentences.i: Once he had tasted it he threw the axe down, and from then on honoured the tree as sacred and tended it.
sentences.n: γεύομαι in the middle is 'take a taste for oneself'. One aorist against two imperfects: ἔρριψε is the single act, ἐτίμα and ἐπεμελεῖτο the standing practice that follows. ἐπιμελέομαι takes the genitive of what one looks after.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οὐ τοσοῦτον οἱ ἄνθρωποι φύσει τὸ δίκαιον ἀγαπῶσι καὶ τιμῶσιν ὅσον τὸ κερδαλέον ἐπιδιώκουσι.
sentences.tr: Hoti ou tosouton hoi anthrōpoi physei to dikaion agapōsi kai timōsin hoson to kerdaleon epidiōkousin.
sentences.l: That men do not by nature love and honour what is just so much as they pursue what is profitable.
sentences.i: The story shows that men do not by nature love and honour what is just so much as they pursue what brings them gain.
sentences.n: A moral opening with a bare Ὅτι: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. τοσοῦτον … ὅσον is the correlative pair, 'so much … as'. φύσει is a dative of respect, 'in point of nature'. τὸ κερδαλέον is the gainful thing, from κέρδος, profit — and τιμῶσιν here is the same verb the farmer's conversion used two lines above.
